stories.headline: Rasmussen shines as Rays beat Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 to take a 3-2 ALCS lead
stories.summary: — Drew Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win, Tampa Bay’s offense kept on constant pressure and the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 Sunday night to take a 3-2 lead in the AL Championship Series.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- — Drew Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win, Tampa Bay’s offense kept on constant pressure and the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 Sunday night to take a 3-2 lead in the AL Championship Series.


The Rays have won the last two games and will try to capture their third AL pennant and first since 2020 on Monday at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.


“Momentum is big in this sport and we have it -- and we’re going to keep it," outfielder Jonny DeLuca said.


Since the ALCS expanded to seven games in 1985, road teams winning Game 5 for a 3-2 lead have won the series four of five times.


Game 7 if needed would be Tuesday, and the World Series starts Friday at NL champion Milwaukee.


Rasmussen gave up four hits, walked one and struck out six.


“The way he limited anything was really, really impressive," Rays manager Kevin Cash said. "He got in rhythm with the fastball. A lot of power to everything. Then the depth on the changeup throughout the outing was a big pitch for him.”


Tampa Bay scored single runs in each of the first three innings, the first two off Parker Messick and the third against Tim Herrin. The Guardians scored in the seventh but stranded runners in the eighth and ninth innings.


Cleveland has not won an ALCS when trailing 3-2 while the Rays are 58-27 at home this year, including the postseason.


The Guardians are seeking their first World Series title since 1948.


“We know we’ve got our work cut out for us. It’s a really good team and a really good team when they play at home, especially," Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. "@e know this is going to be tough but if there’s a group I’m betting on to get this done, it’s our guys.”


Rasmussen with another strong postseason outing
Rasmussen had given up two runs over six innings in the opener. After Chase DeLauter’s two-out single in the first, the 31-year-old right-hander retired nine straight batters and allowed only one other baserunner through the sixth.


“Ras has done it all year, shutting them down like he did tonight," shortstop Taylor Walls said. "Sometimes it’s a little boring when he’s mowing guys down, but it was fun tonight because Cleveland was putting the ball in play. Credit to them for doing that and giving us the chance to make plays.”


Rasmussen said the biggest change was he was able to command his changeup better. He used it only 12 times in Game 1, but threw it 27 times on Sunday, includng 21 for strikes.


“We were able to attack with the change-up a lot more tonight than we did, like I said, in Game 1. The ability to drive the cutter to the top I thought was also another strength,” said Rasmussen, who is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA in three postseason starts, striking out 23 and walking three.


Cam Booser and Tyler Wells worked the eighth, with Wells striking out José Ramírez to strand a runner.


Bryan Baker came in for the ninth and converted his 35th straight save chance, his fifth of this postseason. Jo Adell was on second base when Travis Bazzana hit a game-ending groundout.


Rays take advantage of early opportunities
Tampa Bay’s leadoff hitter reached base in the first four innings — scoring in the first three frames — and six times overall. Rays' leadoff batters have reached in 10 of 14 innings dating to Saturday.


Yandy Díaz had three hits while Aranda and Liam Hicks both had two hits and drove in a run.


Díaz scored on a bases-loaded walk by Messick to Jonny DeLuca in the first inning. Díaz led off with a line-drive double over center fielder Petey Halpin that rolled to the wall.


Aranda’s single drove in Ben Williamson for a 2-0 lead in the second, and Hicks looped a curveball from Herrin to center to score Chandler Simpson in the third.


“I think we took advantage of getting ourselves in some favorable counts and getting some big hits,” Cash said. “We probably left some opportunities out there, and then they go to the bullpen, and it’s really challenging to piece together big innings when they’re mixing and matching from the third or fourth inning, whatever it was, on.”


Kwan helps keep Cleveland in the game
Steven Kwan had two of Cleveland’s five hits and made two fine defensive plays: He threw out Walls trying to score from second base on Jonathan Aranda’s fourth-inning single to left and made a leaping catch at the center-field wall on Victor Mesa Jr.’s eighth-inning drive, saving a run.


Cleveland finally threatened in the seventh when Kwan and Ramírez singled to put runners at the corners and DeLauter grounded an RBI single between first and second.


Messick had the shortest outing of his big league career and didn’t make it past the third inning for the second time in four postseason starts. The 25-year-old left-hander went two innings and allowed two runs, five hits and three walks over two innings, throwing just 34 of 57 pitches for strikes.


Up next
Tampa Bay will go with right-hander Freddy Peralta (1-0, 0.79 ERA), who will make his third appearance of the series. He started Game 2 and threw six scoreless innings before pitching two-thirds of an inning on Saturday. Cleveland has not named a starter, but Vogt ruled out using right-hander Gavin Williams.

stories.headline: Cruel Achilles injury has killed the Ben Simmons comeback Australia was dying to see
stories.summary: For the first time in years, Ben Simmons had given us a reason to believe. That's what made the news of his Achilles injury hit so heavily -- he'd started to answer a question that had followed him for half a decade, Olgun Uluc writes.
stories.body:
For the first time in years, Ben Simmons had given us a reason to believe.

That's what made the news land so heavily. Because it wasn't just that Simmons had torn his Achilles; it was that it happened now, days before the NBA season, just as he'd started to answer a question that had followed him for half a decade.

Every Achilles tear is cruel, but this one felt slightly more unjust than most. For years, the knock on Simmons was that he didn't care enough. He was supposedly a gifted athlete who'd drifted on talent alone; someone who enjoyed the fruits of the game more than the game itself. This comeback was quietly dismantling that idea. He was returning from back injuries that very well should have been debilitating, which isn't something you just 'talent' your way back from that.

So, on the eve of the NBA season, that comeback being cut short by something out of his control was particularly jarring. It robs us of seeing whether the Australian with the greatest peak in the NBA, and someone who had the potential to be an all-time great, could return to that trajectory.

Given what Simmons hasn't done on a basketball court in recent years, it's worth reminding ourselves what he was. As a high school player out of Melbourne, he was the first Australian ever selected for the McDonald's All-American game, widely regarded as the premier exhibition in junior basketball in the U.S. He was the consensus No. 1 player in his class, winning the Naismith, Gatorade and Morgan Wootten national player of the year awards.

I sat with a then-18-year-old Simmons in the bowels of the United Center in Chicago in April, 2015 during McDonald's All American week. Cameras, recruiters, sneaker reps, and reporters filled every corridor, all waiting on the same handful of teenagers. We sat for an interview on the concourse of the arena. Shaquille O'Neal had just called him the best player in the world.

"People can say what they want but, at the end, I have to bring it," Simmons told me at the time.

For all intents and purposes, he did bring it. When he got to the NBA, as the No. 1 overall pick, LeBron James called him 'Young King'. That was apt because, with every big game from Simmons, three names were almost always attached: James, Oscar Robertson, and Magic Johnson.

Simmons became the only rookie ever to average at least 15 points, 8 rebounds, and 8 assists on better than 50% shooting; he was the first rookie since Robertson in 1961 to average 8 rebounds and 8 assists a game. He had 12 triple-doubles as a rookie, second only to Robertson's 26 and ahead of Magic.

Simmons was one of three rookies to reach 1,000 points, 500 rebounds, and 500 assists, alongside - guess who? - Robertson and Magic. There are too many to continue listing them, but it didn't take long for Simmons to earn three straight NBA All-Star selections (2019 to 2021), an All-NBA Third Team selection in 2020, All-Defensive First Team in 2020 and 2021, and the league's steals leader in 2019-20.

As an Australian, he was the first to win NBA Rookie of the Year - and any major NBA award - the first All-Star, and signed the richest contract ever signed by an Australian athlete: a five-year, US$170 million extension in 2019.

No Australian basketballer has reached that peak. In November 2017, nine games into his career, I asked him how long it would take to become the best player in the league.

"Time will tell," he said. "It depends on the work I put in and how great I wanna be."

For all the peaks, there were also some valleys. There was the Game 7 loss to Atlanta in 2021, the trade request, the holdout. Is there regret in how his tenure in Philadelphia ended? It'd be unreasonable to think there wasn't.

What does get lost in the noise is that his back injury was completely legitimate. He hurt it ramping up his conditioning after the trade to the Nets and never played for Brooklyn that season. He had a microdiscectomy for a herniated disc in 2022. A nerve impingement shut him down in March 2023. It returned six games into the next season, and he missed 38 straight games. In March, 2024, he had a second back surgery.

During that period of time, his body wouldn't let him be him.

The Boomers are the harder part in all of this. In Chicago, at 18, he'd told me: "As soon as I'm able to put on that jersey for my country in the Olympics, I'll do it."

He passed on Rio in 2016, which was understandable heading into his rookie season. In May, 2019, healthy and a fresh All-Star, he committed to that year's World Cup, but pulled out two months later, choosing to focus on the Sixers' season while saying he'd still be part of the warmup games at home.

In June 2021, healthy again, he withdrew from the Tokyo Olympics to work on his game after the Atlanta series. He hasn't played for Australia in a major tournament, and there were windows when he absolutely could have played. Had he taken one, he'd have a reservoir of goodwill at home that might have carried him through everything since. Australians forgive almost anything from someone who turns up in green and gold. It also fed the narrative that followed him for years: that he didn't care enough; that he was okay to just coast as a supremely gifted athlete.

Simmons' actions of late have actually told a different story, though. There was the Boomers' player-led camp that he took part in in Melbourne over the offseason, and the workout he took part in ahead of signing with the Sacramento Kings, all as part of the process of overcoming these brutal back injuries.

What's also worth remembering, in light of this Achilles tear, is that we've been here before. Almost to the month.

On September 30, 2016, in the final scrimmage of his first NBA training camp with the Philadelphia 76ers, Simmons rolled his ankle and broke the fifth metatarsal in his right foot. The No. 1 pick lost his entire rookie season before it began. The two injuries both came in practice, both on the eve of a season he'd waited for.

Simmons overcame that broken foot to put together the greatest peak for an Australian in the NBA, and was on the trajectory to be one of the best players in the league. That, to put it lightly, is notable. Yes, Simmons has earned and enjoyed the fruits that come with being an NBA player and celebrity, but he's also experienced some of its pitfalls; and, oftentimes, demonstrated that he can overcome those bouts of adversity, despite the perceived apathy.

Simmons addressed the Achilles injury in a recent social media post: "I've faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically, and emotionally, and I've found a way through every single one of them," he said.

"This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story. It's never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here. But if there's one thing I've learned, it's that adversity doesn't define you. How you respond to it does."

This attempted NBA comeback wasn't just a façade. The way we know that is because we all felt the same pit in the bottom of our stomachs when we saw the news of this injury. We'd all accepted this was a real, honest endeavour for Simmons to get back to the league, and hopefully return to the player he once was. His return had captured the imagination of everyone across the NBA ecosystem.

There's reason to have hope that, like his foot injury as a rookie, this is just a blip; that Simmons has developed the tools to, once again, overcome adversity: "I've been knocked down before, and I've always found a way to get back up," he said. "This time will be no different."

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.

stories.headline: Jasmine Jasudavicius outpoints Erin Blanchfield at UFC Fight Night
stories.summary: Jasmine Jasudavicius stated her case as a contender in the UFC women's featherweight division, dominating Erin Blanchfield on the canvas to win by unanimous decision.
stories.body:
Instability and opportunity permeate the UFC women's flyweight division, which crowned a new champion two weeks ago and has a former two-time champ lurking in the wings while healing from injury. Several other title hopefuls have been jostling to position themselves to go for the gold.

Jasmine Jasudavicius seized the opportunity to make her presence felt among the leading contenders Saturday, dominating Erin Blanchfield on the canvas in a clash of top-10 125-pounders to win by unanimous decision at UFC Fight Night in Edmonton, Alberta.

The fight was the co-main event of a card headlined by Mike Malott's explosive knockout win over Joaquin Buckley. Malott, who like Jasudavicius is from Ontario and had the crowd firmly behind him, landed a knee to the chin that crumbled Buckley, who is No. 8 in the ESPN welterweight rankings and lost his third in a row.

"Hey, guys, I might be soft-spoken," Malott said afterward, "but I'm f---ing hard-hitting."

Malott's knockout came at 2 minutes, 32 seconds of the second round and put a ferocious cap on an event that tied a UFC record with 12 finishes (seven knockouts, five submissions). The other modern-era fight card with a dozen finishes was UFC Fight Night in Belgrade, Serbia, on Aug. 1.

Nevertheless, it was the night's lone bout to go the distance that had the highest stakes. Jasudavicius, No. 8 in the ESPN women's flyweight rankings, pulled off the upset against third-ranked Blanchfield, who came in situated behind only injured former champion Valentina Shevchenko and new titlist Natalia Silva. Blanchfield is also No. 9 in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound top 10.

Jasudavicius (16-4) surely elevated her standing in the 125-pound hierarchy with a robust performance that produced her second straight victory.

Both women came in touted as elite grapplers, and Jasudavicius proved to be a step ahead by repeatedly taking the fight to the ground (five takedowns) and threatening submissions from dominant positions for long stretches of the first two rounds.

"I love grappling," she said. "I understand it. I'm pretty good at it. And I like to show what I've got."

Jasudavicius showed enough to impress the judges, getting the nod on all three scorecards (29-28, 29-28, 29-28). The announcement of the verdict drew a roar from the crowd, which was enthusiastically behind the 37-year-old competing in her home country.

"To be able to fight in Canada, you hear the crowd, man. We're about it," Jasudavicius said.

Jasudavicius and Malott were among a dozen Canadian fighters on the card who went a combined 5-7.

Jasudavicius' victory might not put her in position for an immediate title shot, but she has her sights on a future meeting with the new champion, who defeated her by decision in 2022 in her second UFC fight.

"I want to cross paths with Natalia Silva again," Jasudavicius said. "We had a little bit of history before, so it would be an epic story."

For Blanchfield (14-3), the defeat halted a two-fight winning streak. She outlanded Jasudavicius 62-43 in significant strikes, but the author of five UFC submissions never could get her ground game going. Jasudavicius put Blanchfield on the defensive the whole fight with nearly eight minutes of control time.

stories.headline: Barcelona's Eric García, Jules Koundé ruled out of PSG clash with injury
stories.summary: Eric García and Jules Koundé have both been ruled out of Barcelona's Champions League game against Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday.
stories.body:
Eric García and Jules Koundé have both been ruled out of Barcelona's Champions League game against Paris Saint-Germain on Tuesday.

García will also miss Sunday's Clásico against Real Madrid after being ruled out for up to four weeks with a thigh injury picked up in Saturday's win at Real Betis.

Koundé will be assessed ahead of Madrid's visit to Spotify Camp Nou in LaLiga this weekend after spraining his ankle in the same game.

The loss of García and Koundé leaves Barça coach Hansi Flick without either of the players he has used at right-back this season.

However, João Cancelo and Xavi Espart, both used as left-backs this year, can play there, as could Alejandro Balde.

García's injury also leaves Barça short at centre-back, with Andreas Christensen currently out with a thigh issue, too.

That leaves Pau Cubarsí and Gerard Martín as the only available central defenders in the squad ahead of Tuesday's showdown with the European champions.

Midfielders Rodri and Frenkie de Jong have also played there in the past, with Flick confirming the Dutchman could be an option at the back after he returned to training last week.

Elsewhere, following De Jong's return to the matchday squad at the weekend, Barça are in good shape ahead of the biggest week of their season so far.

Captain Raphinha returned off the bench against Betis and will be available for Tuesday's game in Paris and Madrid's visit on Sunday.

Barça are seeking to maintain their perfect start to the season in France after winning all 11 of their matches in all competitions to date.

stories.headline: How Golden State held court to take 1-0 lead over Atlanta in WNBA Finals
stories.summary: Golden State held court 68-64 to take a 1-0 lead over the Atlanta Dream in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Game 1 goes to the Golden State Valkyries.

The No. 2 seed held court 68-64 in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals to take the early lead over the No. 4 seed Atlanta Dream in the best-of-seven series.

Gabby Williams led Golden State with 26 points, including four free throws in the final 1:18 to seal the victory. The back-and-forth game featured seven lead changes.

Allisha Gray paced the Dream with 19 points but didn't score in the fourth quarter when the Dream shot 2-for-20 in the period. Angel Reese had 14 points and 12 rebounds.

The Valkyries, who have won all five playoff games at home this postseason and had the best record at home in the regular season, snapped the Dream's 10-game winning streak, which dated to the regular season.

Both teams seek their first WNBA championship. Game 2 is Monday night back at Chase Center. As the better seed, the Valkyries will host Games 2 and, if necessary, 5 and 7 in a 2-2-1-1-1 format.

ESPN was courtside Saturday with live analysis throughout the game.

Jump to:

Postgame analysis | Relive the action

More:

Finals preview | Top 15 players | Schedule | Offseason guide

(2) Golden State Valkyries 68,

(4) Atlanta Dream 64

How Golden State won the game: Both teams made big runs in this game, which set up a fourth quarter that was all about grit and determination. And also timing. After being outscored 17-9 in the third quarter, the Valkyries outscored the Dream 17-8 in the fourth quarter.

The Dream went just 4-of-25 from 3-point range, with Allisha Gray going 1-of-8. They were 18-of-21 from the foul line, but that was an area where the Valkyries were able to make up ground in the fourth quarter, finishing 11-of-16 from the stripe.

Getting into crunch time, Atlanta seemed to get a little too sped up offensively and took shots too early when it would have helped the Dream to work their offense more. Of course, that's easier said than done against the best defense in the WNBA.

Rebounding ended up being a key factor, as the Valkyries won the board battle 41-35. And Golden State's depth -- much talked about before the series began -- came through. Particularly with Kaila Charles, who played 30 minutes, compiling seven points and 10 rebounds.

Gabby Williams led the way with 26 points, the only Valkyries player in double figures. -- Michael Voepel

What the win means for the Valkyries: They won their first Finals game in their first WNBA Finals appearance. Even when the Dream went on runs, the Valkyries never deviated from their game plan -- and it never felt like they fully lost momentum. Maybe that's also a credit to the noise in Ballhalla.

This game showed an elite level of composure from the Valkyries, and that is a great sign for Golden State. Gabby Williams said that even though the Valkyries trailed with a few minutes left in the game, they had the Dream "right where we wanted them." She said it's because they knew the game would come down to stops.

"That's our bread and butter," Williams added.

If the Valkyries can withstand the Dream's offensive runs and then lock them up on defense, they have a good chance to head to Atlanta with a 2-0 lead. -- Kendra Andrews

What changes do you expect in Game 2? The Dream must win a game on the road if they want to win the title, so winning Game 1 would have given them more of a cushion moving forward. Now, Game 2 feels like a must-win at Chase Center before the series shifts to Atlanta for Games 3 and 4.

Dream coach Karl Smesko sounded confident in his team's ability to turn things around in Game 2. He said Saturday's game didn't come down to what Golden State did, but rather the Dream's loss was the result of one bad defensive stretch and a cold offensive quarter in the fourth.

Still, when the Dream punched first in the opening quarter, they led by only eight points at the end of the period. For Atlanta to even the series Monday, the Dream have to make sure they are executing. They also need more from Angel Reese, who dominated early but was held scoreless in the second half, and Rhyne Howard, who finished with 12 points but shot 3-for-14 from the field and 2-for-9 from 3-point range. -- Andrews

stories.headline: When can Kimi Antonelli win the F1 title? Earliest date, points needed and remaining races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by 102 points in the standings with a maximum of 150 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he could be crowned champion as early as Oct. 24 at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, but the maths around that calculation are slightly complicated by question marks over the final two races of the season. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 125 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would change the maths around the championship fight, making it easier for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Austin.

- 'Chucky' Verstappen is back. Luckily for Antonelli and Mercedes, it's too late

- Max Verstappen takes back-to-back wins with dominant drive at Singapore GP

- Lewis Hamilton calls Singapore GP strategy 'painful lesson' after Ferrari apology

Alongside Russell and Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris are still mathematically in contention for this year's championship, although the incredibly slim hopes of Leclerc and Norris would be snuffed out entirely by the cancellation of the races in the Middle East.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Austin?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Austin remain relatively slim. The Mercedes driver would need to win in Texas, with his teammate Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton finishing fifth or lower.

Such a scenario would put Antonelli 125 points ahead of Russell with 125 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Austin, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories (by that stage Antonelli would be on nine and Russell on three with five races remaining).

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli would only need to leave Austin with a lead of 100 points over his rivals.

Such a scenario would result in the following permutations:

If Antonelli wins in Austin he would be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish.
If Antonelli finishes second, he would be crowned champion if Russell doesn't win the race.
If Antonelli finishes third, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes off the podium.
If Antonelli finishes fourth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes behind him and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes fifth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fourth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes sixth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes fifth or lower and Hamilton does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes seventh, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes sixth or lower and Hamilton does not finish in the top two.
If Antonelli finishes eighth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes seventh or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top two and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes ninth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes eighth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton does not finish in the top three and Verstappen does not win the race.
If Antonelli fails to score, he would be crowned champion if Russell finishes ninth or lower, Hamilton finishes fifth or lower and Verstappen does not win the race.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs 49 points over the remaining rounds, which could be achieved with as little as five sixth place finishes and one fifth place finish over the rest of the season.

If only five races remain, Antonelli would need just 24 points to secure the title, which would be attainable with two seventh place finishes and three eighth place finishes at the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: Lionel Messi scores twice, takes season tally to 25 in Miami win at Atlanta
stories.summary: Lionel Messi scored two scintillating second-half solo goals to take his MLS-leading tally to 25 as Inter Miami brushed aside hosts Atlanta United 3-1 on Saturday.
stories.body:
Lionel Messi scored two trademark second-half solo goals to take his MLS-leading tally to 25 as Inter Miami brushed aside hosts Atlanta United 3-1 on Saturday.

After Mexico striker Germán Berterame put Miami ahead in the 45th minute, Messi took center stage after the restart with two goals in four minutes.

The first, in the 56th minute, came after Messi drove infield from the right wing and exchanged passes with Berterame on the edge off the penalty area before dancing past a desperate Atlanta defender and firing low into the net.

His second was more of the same. This time, Luis Suárez sent him free on a breakaway and the Argentine forward again bewitched a hapless defender before once more beating Atlanta goalkeeper Lucas Hoyos with his left foot.

Atlanta got a late consolation goal through a penalty from former Miami forward Fafà Picault.

"He never ceases to amaze the world," Miami coach Cristian "Kily" González said of Messi afterward. "I mean, I honestly can't believe that a guy like him, at 39 years old, is doing what he's doing. And what makes me happiest is seeing that he's truly happy. Because he's happy, he gives everything he has. He enjoys himself and feels right at home.

"As I always say, he pushes us to be better every single day. It's an immense joy to have him here. Everyone knows how special our relationship is. Every time I see him, he brings a smile to my face. I'm still constantly amazed by him."

At full time of Saturday's game, Messi had a six-goal lead in the race for MLS' Golden Boot and also had the joint-most assists (15), along with LAFC's Son Heung-Min, having been credited with a secondary assist on Berterame's opener.

Messi is the first player in MLS history to register 15 assists in three consecutive seasons. He now has a goal contribution in 13 straight matches, tying his second-longest streak with club and country in his career.

Saturday's brace also took Messi to 936 career goals, and his coach has no doubts that he can reach the 1,000 milestone.

"Yes, I believe he'll reach 1,000 goals," González said. "I have faith in that. I know he will, because he loves a challenge, he sets challenges for himself and since he's already achieved everything else, this will be no exception."

He added: "He dazzles me with every single action, every time I see him in training. I truly hope he continues to amaze us right up until the day he decides to retire, which, hopefully, won't be for a long time yet."

Messi's performance Saturday gave the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner another fond memory at Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The game marked Messi's first visit there since the 2026 World Cup semifinal in July, when he provided two late assists to propel Argentina to a dramatic win over England.

Messi has four goals in three games since he bid farewell to the Argentina national team in a friendly against Benin earlier this month.

Miami, which clinched a spot in the playoffs Wednesday, has won three straight games and is second in the Eastern Conference behind runaway leader Nashville.

Atlanta, under Gerardo "Tata" Martino, Messi's former coach with Miami and Argentina, is languishing in the 14th spot in the Eastern Conference and facing an uphill battle to make the postseason.

Miami will return to action with a visit to the New York Red Bulls next Saturday.

ESPN's Lizzy Becherano contributed to this report.

stories.headline: RLWC: What we learned from the opening round
stories.summary: Australia survived an opening-night scare, Tonga delivered a historic victory and Samoa wasted little time showcasing their attacking firepower. Isaac Issa takes a look atthe opening weekend of action.
stories.body:
Australia survived an opening-night scare, Tonga delivered a historic victory and Samoa wasted little time showcasing their attacking firepower.

The opening round of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup provided an early look at the contenders, while leaving England facing a difficult path to the knockout stages.

Here are the biggest takeaways from Week 1.

Australia win, but leave room for encouragement for their rivals

Australia banked the result they needed against New Zealand, but their 24-22 victory offered plenty for their rivals to work with.

The Kiwis gained close to 300 more running metres than the Kangaroos, exposing an area Australia will need to address as the tournament progresses. Winning a tight contest is valuable; consistently conceding that much ground is a difficult way to defend a World Cup.

Jack Bostock's debut hat trick proved decisive, while Reece Walsh's long-range try underlined Australia's ability to turn a game through individual brilliance. Those threats remain even when the Kangaroos are struggling to establish control.

For New Zealand, the frustration is that a strong performance went unrewarded. Kalyn Ponga's two tries demonstrated what he can add to their attack, although the arm injury that ended his night and left him needing surgery, raises concerns.

Australia emerged with the points. New Zealand showed enough to suggest another meeting would be far from straightforward.

Tonga's defence gives their title challenge substance

Tonga's attacking talent attracts attention, but their defensive resolve was the most significant feature of their 30-12 victory over England.

Repeatedly challenged in the opening half, Kristian Woolf's side held England scoreless and reached the break ahead 10-0. When AJ Brimson's try narrowed the gap, Tonga responded with consecutive tries to regain control.

Haumole Olakau'atu finished with a double as Tonga recorded their first victory over England.

The result strengthens their position in the race for a semifinal berth, but the manner of the performance should be just as encouraging.

Tonga demonstrated they could absorb pressure, withstand a shift in momentum and take their opportunities. Those qualities will become increasingly valuable when the tournament reaches its decisive matches.

Their ability with the ball was already apparent. Holding England out through that opening period provided a stronger indication of how difficult they could be to beat.

England already have little margin for error

One defeat has left England facing the prospect of an early exit, even if they win both remaining pool matches.

Only two teams from the combined Pool B and C standings advance to the semifinals. Tonga now hold the head-to-head advantage over England, while Samoa's 78-4 win over France has established a substantial points-difference buffer.

England still have France and Papua New Guinea to play. Winning those fixtures is the immediate requirement, but the size of those victories could also become crucial.

That creates a difficult balance: chasing points while correcting the errors that undermined their opener.

England generated opportunities against Tonga, yet too often failed to turn them into scoreboard pressure. Against opposition capable of punishing those missed chances, promising passages were insufficient.

Their next two performances must deliver considerably more. Even then, qualification could depend on results elsewhere.

Fa'alogo highlights Samoa's enviable attacking depth

Sua Fa'alogo began Samoa's World Cup opener on the bench. He finished it with four tries and 252 running metres.

Introduced after Deine Mariner suffered a hamstring injury, the Melbourne speedster immediately demonstrated the value of Samoa's attacking depth in their 78-4 win over France.

With Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow starting at fullback, Samoa could still call upon another explosive runner capable of transforming an opportunity into points. Fa'alogo's performance gives coach Ben Gardiner plenty to consider as the opposition becomes stronger.

There was encouragement beyond the established names, too. Test debutant Francis Manuleleua ran for 223 metres, including 89 after contact, while Jermaine McEwen topped Samoa's tackle count.

France offered limited resistance, so the result alone cannot establish where Samoa sit among the leading contenders.

It did, however, show how many attacking options they possess, and how difficult selection could become if their emerging players continue to contribute alongside their stars.

stories.headline: Rays beat Guardians in Game 5 behind Drew Rasmussen to take 3-2 ALCS lead
stories.summary: Drew Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win, Tampa Bay's offense kept on constant pressure and the Rays beat the Guardians 3-1 on Sunday night to take a 3-2 lead in the ALCS.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- Drew Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win, Tampa Bay's offense kept on constant pressure and the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 Sunday night to take a 3-2 lead in the AL Championship Series.

The Rays have won the last two games and will try to capture their third AL pennant and first since 2020 on Monday at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.

"Momentum is big in this sport and we have it -- and we're going to keep it," outfielder Jonny DeLuca said.

Since the ALCS expanded to seven games in 1985, road teams winning Game 5 for a 3-2 lead have won the series four of five times.

Game 7 if needed would be Tuesday, and the World Series starts Friday at NL champion Milwaukee.

Rasmussen gave up four hits, walked one and struck out six.

"The way he limited anything was really, really impressive," Rays manager Kevin Cash said. "He got in rhythm with the fastball. A lot of power to everything. Then the depth on the changeup throughout the outing was a big pitch for him."

Tampa Bay scored single runs in each of the first three innings, the first two off Parker Messick and the third against Tim Herrin. The Guardians scored in the seventh but stranded runners in the eighth and ninth innings.

Cleveland has not won an ALCS when trailing 3-2 while the Rays are 58-27 at home this year, including the postseason.

The Guardians are seeking their first World Series title since 1948.

"We know we've got our work cut out for us. It's a really good team and a really good team when they play at home, especially," Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said. "We know this is going to be tough but if there's a group I'm betting on to get this done, it's our guys."

Rasmussen had given up two runs over six innings in the opener. After Chase DeLauter's two-out single in the first, the 31-year-old right-hander retired nine straight batters and allowed only one other baserunner through the sixth.

"Ras has done it all year, shutting them down like he did tonight," shortstop Taylor Walls said. "Sometimes it's a little boring when he's mowing guys down, but it was fun tonight because Cleveland was putting the ball in play. Credit to them for doing that and giving us the chance to make plays."

Rasmussen said the biggest change was he was able to command his changeup better. He used it only 12 times in Game 1, but threw it 27 times on Sunday, including 21 for strikes.

"We were able to attack with the change-up a lot more tonight than we did, like I said, in Game 1. The ability to drive the cutter to the top I thought was also another strength," said Rasmussen, who is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA in three postseason starts, striking out 23 and walking three.

Cam Booser and Tyler Wells worked the eighth, with Wells striking out Jose Ramirez to strand a runner.

Bryan Baker came in for the ninth and converted his 35th straight save chance, his fifth of this postseason. Jo Adell was on second base when Travis Bazzana hit a game-ending groundout.

Tampa Bay's leadoff hitter reached base in the first four innings -- scoring in the first three frames -- and six times overall. Rays leadoff batters have reached in 10 of 14 innings dating to Saturday.

Yandy Diaz had three hits while Aranda and Liam Hicks both had two hits and drove in a run.

Díaz scored on a bases-loaded walk by Messick to DeLuca in the first inning. Díaz led off with a line-drive double over center fielder Petey Halpin that rolled to the wall.

Aranda's single drove in Ben Williamson for a 2-0 lead in the second, and Hicks looped a curveball from Herrin to center to score Chandler Simpson in the third.

"I think we took advantage of getting ourselves in some favorable counts and getting some big hits," Cash said. "We probably left some opportunities out there, and then they go to the bullpen, and it's really challenging to piece together big innings when they're mixing and matching from the third or fourth inning, whatever it was, on."

Steven Kwan had two of Cleveland's five hits and made two fine defensive plays: He threw out Walls trying to score from second base on Jonathan Aranda's fourth-inning single to left and made a leaping catch at the center-field wall on Victor Mesa Jr.'s eighth-inning drive, saving a run.

Cleveland finally threatened in the seventh when Kwan and Ramírez singled to put runners at the corners and DeLauter grounded an RBI single between first and second.

Messick had the shortest outing of his big league career and didn't make it past the third inning for the second time in four postseason starts. The 25-year-old left-hander went two innings and allowed two runs, five hits and three walks over two innings, throwing just 34 of 57 pitches for strikes.

Tampa Bay will go with right-hander Freddy Peralta (1-0, 0.79 ERA), who will make his third appearance of the series. He started Game 2 and threw six scoreless innings before pitching two-thirds of an inning on Saturday. Cleveland has not named a starter, but Vogt ruled out using right-hander Gavin Williams.

stories.headline: Warriors' Stephen Curry 'fine' after tweaking right ankle in practice
stories.summary: Steve Kerr said franchise superstar Stephen Curry is "fine" after he limped off the practice court with a right ankle issue.
stories.body:
Golden State Warriors superstar guard Stephen Curry tweaked his right ankle during the team's open practice in San Francisco on Sunday night, limping to the locker room.

Coach Steve Kerr told reporters afterward that Curry avoided a major issue.

Curry was lined up against reserve guard De'Anthony Melton on the wing when he showed frustration after a slip and misstep, banging the basketball on the floor. Action stopped and Curry's teammates expressed immediate concern at his discomfort. Several staffers went down the tunnel to visit Curry, including Kerr.

"He's fine," Kerr said.

Curry missed 43 games last season, including 27 for persistent pain and swelling in his right knee. The Warriors have purposefully ramped up Curry's court work slower this season, lightening his practice time and minutes in the preseason. He turns 39 in March.

There is no immediate word on Curry's status, but a team source reiterated the ankle tweak is "not serious."

The Warriors open the season Wednesday night in Los Angeles against the Lakers.

stories.summary: — Kirill Kaprizov broke a second-period tie with his NHL-leading 10th goal, Jesper Wallstedt stopped 13 shots and the Minnesota Wild beat the Columbus Blue Jackets 2-1 on Sunday night.
stories.body:
ST. PAUL, Minn. -- — Kirill Kaprizov broke a second-period tie with his NHL-leading 10th goal, Jesper Wallstedt stopped 13 shots and the Minnesota Wild beat the Columbus Blue Jackets 2-1 on Sunday night.


Danila Yurov also scored to help the Central Division-leading Wild improve to 6-2-1.


Adam Fantilli scored for Columbus. Cam Talbot made 32 saves.


Kaprizov broke a 1-1 tie with a power-play goal at 3:06 of the second, beating Talbot over the shoulder from the bottom of the left faceoff circle.


Both goalies stood tall early in the first period. Wallstedt denied Connor Garland on a breakaway two minutes into the game. Then Talbot made three saves as the Blue Jackets killed off a 5-on-3 power play that lasted 1:52.


Minnesota got on the board late in the first period. Yakov Trenin scooped up a turnover at the Columbus blue line, beat a defender on the way to the net, then feathered a pass across the slot where Yurov was waiting to tap it in.


Columbus tied it a minute later during a delayed penalty when Fantilli fired a slap shot through traffic that beat Wallstedt.

stories.headline: Lisandro Martínez's Man United comments 'not that far off' but should not have been made - Peter Schmeichel
stories.summary: Former Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel has said he believes Lisandro Martínez's criticism of the club's hierarchy is "not that far off."
stories.body:
Former Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel has said he believes Lisandro Martínez's criticism of the club's hierarchy is "not that far off" but added he would not have liked hearing a teammate sound off in public.

Schmeichel was criticised for his handling of a post-match interview with Martínez in the aftermath of Tuesday night's 2-0 Champions League loss to Atlético Madrid, when the Argentina defender turned his fire on the club's hierarchy and named director of football Jason Wilcox as one of those from whom he "expects more."

Martínez spoke first to Amazon Prime's Gabriel Clarke before Schmeichel interviewed him for U.S. broadcaster CBS, with the defender repeating many of his criticisms while Schmeichel appeared to be trying to move Martínez on from the topic.

On Thursday Martínez issued a public apology for his comments and United said the matter was considered closed after the 28-year-old met with manager Michael Carrick, Wilcox and the club's hierarchy.

But inevitably the issue dominated Carrick's news conference on Friday with the substance of Martínez's comments still being debated.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily, Schmeichel said: "I would not like any teammate ever to go out and talk like that. Unless it was Bryan Robson... No, I wouldn't. I absolutely wouldn't like that.

"In the dressing rooms I was in, you were accountable. It just didn't happen very often that somebody stepped out of line, and of course we had a manager [Sir Alex Ferguson] who would not allow you to step out of line. He would react to that straight away...

"It's not that I completely disagree with what [Martínez] says. That's the other thing."

- Man United 'a circus' amid Lisandro Martínez rant - Roy Keane

Schmeichel then added: "Without going into too much detail about what Martínez said, some of the things he said are not far off.

"Look at the promising teams: Manchester City a long time ago, Arsenal for the past six years, Liverpool under Jürgen Klopp -- what did they do that suddenly changed the dynamics and changed their fortunes? They started at the back.

"They got in a goalkeeper, back four, a centre midfield player. They built that foundation, made it solid, and then they started to bring the creative players in. They've all done it... Built from the back. We've done the opposite, built from the front."

stories.headline: Christian Horner plays down Ferrari links, 'no idea' on Formula 1 return
stories.summary: Christian Horner again played down links to Ferrari as the former Red Bull boss claimed he would be "at peace" if a return to Formula One never happens.
stories.body:
Christian Horner again played down links to Ferrari as the former Red Bull boss claimed he would be "at peace" if a return to Formula One never happens.

Horner, 52, started his speaking tour to help launch his new book, entitled "Drive," at the Barbican in York on Saturday.

He ran through his entire Formula One career, from Red Bull's introduction into the sport through to his controversial exit after the British Grand Prix in 2025.

- Horner: Mercedes' Wolff has it 'easy' at the moment

- Rafael Câmara to Haas: How F1's next rookie could shake up Ferrari's future

- Verstappen finishes 9th in GT World Challenge

But the two-hour show passed without a single mention of the allegations Horner faced during his latter days with the team. The billed Q&A from the audience was delivered in the form of QR-code submitted questions put to Horner by the host.

Red Bull's decision to sack him came a year and a half after he was accused of "inappropriate behaviour" by a female colleague. Horner always denied the accusations and was exonerated for a second time of controlling behaviour by an independent KC. It is a subject covered in the book in a chapter titled "Out come the wolves."

Horner's Red Bull exit ended a 20-year career with the team, where he won eight drivers' and six constructors' titles, and he continues to be linked with a return to the sport.

A recent interview, in which Horner described Ferrari as the biggest brand in F1, reignited links to the Italian giants, but he again moved to talk that down.

"I said 'there's an aura around Ferrari, it's a privilege as a driver, an engineer etc. It is the dream of so many drivers.' I never said it was my bloody dream!" Horner said.

"But the story came out that Ferrari was my dream job. I felt sorry for Fred [Vasseur, Ferrari team principal] because suddenly he was under a lot of pressure."

Horner touched on how he lured design guru Adrian Newey to the team, his relationship with world champion drivers Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen and how the organisation of the team changed following the death of Red Bull co-founder Dietrich Mateschitz in 2022.

He described his sacking from Red Bull, days after the Silverstone race, as "brutal."

When the subject of his future came up again, Horner suggested that a return to F1 is not a certainty.

"What excites me most is what is the next chapter going to be and, honestly, I have no idea," Horner added.

"If my time is done in Formula One, I've had a hell of a ride and I did OK. If the right thing comes up to go back, I go back. But I am at peace in myself that if it doesn't I don't have to."

Red Bull are using their own power trains for the first time this season, the culmination of a five-year project launched in 2021 and overseen by Horner until his departure.

Verstappen has won the last two races -- in Malaysia and Singapore -- to deliver the first successes of that project on track and Horner spoke of his pride in seeing the engine come to fruition.

"Seeing that engine come to life and deliver and be reliable ... people thought it would be a joke," he said.

"To see podiums and then the victories in the last two weeks, in its 16th race to win a Grand Prix, I took huge pride in that. Both shareholders contacted me and thanked me."

The 2026 Rugby League Cup kicks off in Sydney with the Kangaroos facing the Kiwis of New Zealand, in what could well be an early preview of the final.

With the continuing growth of International Rugby League and the improving strength of the island nations, each World Cup throws up a tougher challenge.

This year, with the men's, women's and wheelchair competitions to be played across Australia and Papua New Guinea, Australia's long standing rugby league dominance is under serious threat.
